target: Cross-check: Gerstgrasser Accumulate vs Dohmatob Strong Collapse
outcome: Key divergence: Gerstgrasser [D] proves finite upper bound on test error under accumulate strategy (model collapse avoided), while Dohmatob 2024c [E] shows even 1% synthetic data can cause strong collapse. Resolution: [D] accumulates ALL original data, diluting synthetic fraction over time (synthetic proportion shrinks as n grows); [E] mixes at a fixed non-vanishing synthetic proportion. These address different asymptotic regimes: vanishing vs non-vanishing synthetic fraction. Per [E] Section 1.1, collapse can only be avoided if synthetic fraction asymptotically vanishes.

target: [G] Kang et al. 2510.01631 Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training (EMNLP 2025)
outcome: Fetched abstract via arXiv API. Large-scale study (1000+ LLMs, 100k+ GPU hours) comparing natural web data vs synthetic data types (rephrased text, generated textbooks) and mixtures. target: Claim H1: Kovač et al. 2504.03814 lexical diversity amplifies distribution shift
outcome: Claim: Kovač et al. (EMNLP 2025 Oral) provided the first empirical examination of how human training data properties modulate distribution shift magnitude in recursive LLM training loops. Their key finding is that lexical diversity of the human training data amplifies distribution shifts (model collapse), while semantic diversity and data quality mitigate them. Furthermore, these influences are highly modular: data scraped from one internet domain has little influence on content generated for another domain, suggesting different parts of the internet may undergo different types of distribution shift. target: Claim I1: Xu et al. 2505.13947 superlinear sample size growth prevents collapse
outcome: Claim: Xu et al. (2025) conceptualize recursive parametric model training as a random walk of the model estimate and rigorously prove that progressively increasing the sample size at each training step is necessary to prevent model collapse. Under unbiased estimation, the required growth rate follows a superlinear pattern (faster than linear). When estimation bias is present, this required growth rate must be accelerated even further. This provides a precise mathematical condition for collapse avoidance that complements Gerstgrasser et al.'s [D] accumulate strategy. [I, Abstract]
summary_en: Claim I1: Xu et al. 2025. Probabilistic random walk model shows superlinear sample size growth is necessary to prevent model collapse under unbiased estimation. Bias requires even faster growth.

They further extend these results to general parametric model families in an asymptotic regime. [I, Abstract]

target: [H] Claim H1: SWE-Bench-Verified scores may reflect training recall, not issue-solving skill
outcome: CLAIM: SWE-Bench-Verified, the de facto benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on GitHub issue resolution, is likely contaminated with training data. Models performed 3 times better on SWE-Bench-Verified than on comparably structured benchmarks (BeetleBox, SWE-rebench). Most critically, models were 6 times better at identifying edited files using only issue text — a task that should be logically impossible without prior exposure to the specific issues during training. This strongly suggests benchmark scores reflect training recall rather than genuine issue-solving skill, undermining the validity of leaderboard rankings and favoring agents using models with training data overlap. [H, Abstract]

target: [I] Claim I1: Agent success depends on problem-solving strategies and approximate modifications
outcome: CLAIM: An empirical trajectory analysis of 3 state-of-the-art code agents (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus) on SWE-Bench reveals that agent success depends more on problem-solving strategy than model capability alone. Successful agents employ distinct strategies such as defensive programming and thorough context gathering. Failed trajectories are consistently longer and exhibit higher variance than successful ones. 72-81% of failed trajectories still correctly identify problematic files, indicating that fault localization is not the primary bottleneck — rather, success depends on achieving approximate (rather than exact) code modifications and avoiding error accumulation over long trajectories. Failure patterns differ significantly between agent architectures, suggesting that scaffold design shapes failure modes. [I, Abstract]

target: [J] Claim J1: Context management as callable tool significantly improves long-horizon SWE agent performance
outcome: CLAIM: CAT (Context as a Tool) introduces a paradigm elevating context maintenance to a callable tool integrated into agent decision-making. This addresses a critical bottleneck in long-horizon SWE agents: append-only context leads to context explosion and semantic drift. CAT formalizes three components (stable task semantics, condensed long-term memory, high-fidelity short-term interactions) and enables proactive compression at milestones. The resulting model SWE-Compressor achieves 57.6% solved rate on SWE-Bench-Verified, significantly outperforming ReAct-based agents and static compression baselines, while maintaining stable reasoning under bounded context budgets. [J, Abstract]

target: [H] Claim H2: Benchmark contamination calls into question SWE-Bench's ability to measure real-world generalizability
outcome: CLAIM: The contamination evidence in [H] directly extends and sharpens Run 1 Claim 6 (benchmark overestimation). While [C] identified SWE-bench Lite issues with misleading descriptions and exact ground truth patches, [H] provides direct evidence of data contamination: models are 6x better at finding edited files from issue text alone — a task described as 'logically impossible' without prior exposure. This means SWE-Bench-Verified scores may systematically overestimate real-world generalization ability.
